input: The goal of this worked example is to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe and to determine, on the basis of that calculation, what the flow regime is. The Reynolds number, which is a dimensionless quantity denoted by Re, provides a highly useful way of characterising the flow, and it is computed from the density rho (in kg m-3), the mean velocity v (in m s-1), the pipe diameter D (in m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (in Pa s), using the relationship Re = rho v D / mu. For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is equal to 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity mu is equal to 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. In the present example, the pipe diameter D is 0.025 m and the mean velocity v is 2 m s-1. Substituting these values into the expression gives Re = 998 x 2 x 0.025 / 0.001, and carrying out the arithmetic (the numerator, 998 x 2 x 0.025, comes to 49.9, which is then divided by 0.001) yields a Reynolds number of Re = 49900. In order to interpret this result, it is important to recall the standard thresholds: the flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, it is turbulent when the Reynolds number is above Re = 4000, and between these two values the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned by the number alone. Since the computed value of 49900 stands well above the threshold of 4000, the flow in this case can confidently be described as turbulent, and the transitional range between 2300 and 4000 plays no part in the conclusion.
target: Compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe, and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) compares the inertial effect in the flow with the viscous effect, and it is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. The units cancel in the ratio, and the Reynolds number is dimensionless. For water at 293 K, rho is 998 kg m-3 and mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Take D as 0.025 m and v as 2 m s-1. Substitution gives Re = 998 x 2 x 0.025 / 0.001. The numerator, 998 x 2 x 0.025, is 49.9, and division by 0.001 gives Re = 49900. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between 2300 and 4000 the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value of 49900 stands far above 4000, outside the transitional range and clear of its upper boundary, so the flow is turbulent. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself: the value stands well clear of the upper boundary, so no plausible rounding in the inputs moves the assignment. The same computation serves for any liquid in a circular pipe once the four inputs are stated, and the same thresholds carry the assignment. What changes from case to case is only the margin between the computed value and the boundaries, and it is the margin, rather than the value alone, that decides how much trust the assignment deserves.
